Achterberg). No abstract or open copy found.

title: Branching rules revisited
contribution: [inferred from title] Journal version (Oper. Res. Lett. 2005) of ZIB-Report 04-13 on rules for choosing the branching variable; the report was read in full as R002 (card c01). No journal abstract reachable.

title: MIPLIB 2003
contribution: [inferred from title] Journal version (Oper. Res. Lett. 2006) of ZIB-Report 05-28, which presents the 2003 edition of the MIPLIB library; the report was read in full as R005 (card c02). No journal abstract reachable.

title: Teaching MIP Modeling and Solving
contribution: [inferred from title] Two-page OR/MS Today piece (December 2006, Issues in Education column) on teaching MIP modelling and solving; companion of ZIB-Report 06-23, read in full as R007 (card s01). No abstract exists; the article text is open on a Wayback capture (not used).

title: Conflict analysis in mixed integer programming
contribution: [inferred from title] Journal version (Discrete Optim. 2007) of ZIB-Report 05-19, which carries SAT conflict analysis over to MIP; the report was read in full as R004 (card c02). The journal text is in Elsevier's open archive, but ScienceDirect refused scripted access (HTTP 403).

title: Improving the feasibility pump
contribution: [inferred from title] Journal version (Discrete Optim. 2007) of ZIB-Report 05-42, a modification of the feasibility pump; the report was read in full as R006 (card c02). The open-archive journal PDF refused scripted access (HTTP 403).

title: A Dynamic Load Balancing Mechanism for New ParaLEX
contribution: A new load balancing mechanism for ParaLEX, the authors' parallel extension of the CPLEX MIP optimizer, whose simple load balancing did not scale; preliminary results call it efficient on many instance classes (abstract).
problem_entry: ParaLEX had run 30 solver parallelizations efficiently, but its simple load balancing did not clearly scale (abstract).
key_idea: A new (dynamic) load balancing mechanism for a new ParaLEX version; the mechanism is not described in the abstract (abstract).
assumptions: MIPs solved by CPLEX inside the parallel extension ParaLEX (abstract).
experiments: Preliminary computational results on many instance classes; test set, baselines and core counts not stated (abstract).
positioning: Continues the authors' earlier ParaLEX work (abstract).
writing: Hedged result sentence: preliminary, quite efficient, a lot of classes (abstract).
limits_future: Not stated in the abstract. Later use: ParaSCIP introduces its collecting mode as similar to this paper's (R014 p. 7; ref. [17], R014 p. 14).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: thin layer over the mature engine
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Weak: ParaLEX is a parallel extension of the CPLEX MIP optimizer running 30 solvers in parallel; the abstract does not say whether CPLEX runs unmodified. Existing candidate (cards c04, s02).

quotes.text: On the other hand, the simple load balancing mechanism of ParaLEX did not obviously have scalability.
Preliminary computational results show that the load balancing mechanism is quite efficient in solving a lot of classes of problem instances.

title: Constraint Integer Programming: A New Approach to Integrate CP and MIP
contribution: Introduces constraint integer programming (CIP), a generalization of MIP with CP-style general constraints, supported by the SCIP framework (which also integrates SAT techniques), and demonstrates it on pure MIPs and on chip design verification (abstract).
problem_entry: Combine CP and MIP methodologies; CIP generalizes MIP by admitting general constraints as in CP (abstract).
key_idea: In one framework (SCIP, which also integrates SAT techniques), apply the MIP machinery to the linear part and CP techniques to the non-linear constraints (abstract).
assumptions: CIP: MIP plus general constraints; chip verification problems with highly non-linear constraint types (abstract).
proof_devices: SCIP framework integrating CP, MIP and SAT techniques: linear part to the MIP machinery, non-linear constraints to CP techniques (abstract)
experiments: Pure MIPs: SCIP called almost competitive with commercial MIP solvers; chip verification: CIP called very effective; no numbers in the abstract (abstract). R009's card (c02) finds the first claim rests on solved counts while CPLEX is at least 10 % faster on 27 of 36 instances.
positioning: CIP presented as a novel way to combine CP and MIP (abstract).

method_links.note: Abstract level: CP's general constraints and SAT techniques brought into a MIP framework. The data-structure level and the per-habit tests are in R009 (c02), not in the abstract. Same paper as R009.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: linearize only what stays small, propagate the rest
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: MIP machinery for the linear part, CP techniques for the non-linear constraints. Existing candidate from R009; same paper, not a new occurrence.

transferable: For a model with a large linear core and a few constraint types that linearize badly, keep the LP relaxation for the linear part and handle the rest by propagation in the same search (abstract).
coauthors: Timo Berthold, Thorsten Koch, Kati Wolter

quotes.text: CIP is a generalization of MIP that supports the notion of general constraints as in CP.

The CIP approach is very effective here: it can apply the full sophisticated MIP machinery to the linear part of the problem, while dealing with the non-linear constraints by employing constraint programming techniques.

title: Counting Solutions of Integer Programs Using Unrestricted Subtree Detection
contribution: Extends branch-and-cut IP frameworks to generate all feasible solutions by detecting unrestricted subtrees, which prunes the search tree and collects several solutions at once (branch-and-count) (abstract).
problem_entry: Algorithms find optimal IP solutions, but applications such as hardware and software verification and discrete geometry may want or need all feasible solutions (abstract).
key_idea: Detect unrestricted subtrees to prune the search tree and collect several solutions simultaneously (abstract).
assumptions: Integer programs; generation of all feasible solutions (abstract).
experiments: Computational results said to show the potential of the detection; test set not stated (abstract).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: mirror pruning for a new task
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A second prune rule (unrestricted subtrees) serves the counting task. Existing candidate from R010; same paper.

transferable: To make an optimizer enumerate, add a prune rule for subtrees whose solutions can all be collected in one step (abstract); R010 p. 4 gives the test (every constraint locally redundant at the node).

quotes.text: In many applications it is, however, desirable (or even necessary) to generate all feasible solutions.
We propose a method to detect so-called unrestricted subtrees, which allows us to prune the integer program search tree and to collect several solutions simultaneously.

title: Hybrid Branching
contribution: Hybrid branching, a branching-variable selection rule that combines selection rules from CSP, MIP and SAT (abstract).
problem_entry: Branching on single variables is very common in CSP, MIP and SAT, but the rules for choosing the variable differ significantly (abstract).
key_idea: Combine the selection rules of all three fields in one rule; the combination is not described in the abstract (abstract).
assumptions: Branch-and-bound solvers that branch on individual variables (abstract).
positioning: Puts CSP, MIP and SAT branching side by side (abstract).

method_links.note: Selection rules from CSP and SAT joined with MIP's in one rule; the test is not described in the abstract.

transferable: When neighbouring solver fields answer the same subproblem differently (here: which variable to branch on), try one rule that combines their criteria instead of picking one field's rule (abstract).

quotes.text: Branching on individual variables is very common in CSP, MIP, and SAT.
In this paper, we present hybrid branching, which combines selection rules from all three fields.

title: Integration of AI and OR Techniques in Constraint Programming for Combinatorial Optimization Problems - 8th International Conference, CPAIOR 2011, Berlin, Germany, May 23-27, 2011. Proceedings
contribution: Co-edited, with J. Christopher Beck, the refereed proceedings of CPAIOR 2011 in Berlin: 13 full and 7 short papers and 3 invited lectures selected from 35 submissions (abstract).
positioning: Conference focus: integrating CP, AI and OR for large, complex combinatorial optimization problems (abstract).
writing: Publisher's book description; its author is not stated.

quotes.text: The 13 revised full papers and 7 revised short papers presented together with 3 invited lectures were carefully reviewed and selected from 35 submissions.

title: Hybrid Solving Techniques
contribution: Survey chapter, with Andrea Lodi, on the algorithmic side of CP-OR hybridization (hybrid solving) (abstract).
problem_entry: Hybrid methods over 10-15 years of CP-OR relations, in three contexts: hybrid modeling, hybrid solving and hybrid software tools (abstract).
key_idea: Concentrate on hybrid solving, the algorithmic side (abstract).
positioning: Chapter in a volume on ten years of CPAIOR (metadata).

quotes.text: Three main hybridization contexts have been explored: hybrid modeling, hybrid solving (algorithmic methods) and hybrid software tools.
In this chapter we concentrate on the algorithmic side of the hybridization.

title: ParaSCIP: A Parallel Extension of SCIP
contribution: ParaSCIP, a distributed-memory parallelization of SCIP that runs SCIP solvers as independent processes on subproblems; it solved two previously unsolved MIPLIB 2003 instances on up to 2048 cores of HLRN II (abstract).
problem_entry: Parallelize the MIP solver SCIP on a distributed-memory computing environment (abstract).
key_idea: SCIP solvers run as independent processes that solve subproblems locally, so the parallel code is developed independently of SCIP and profits from future SCIP versions (abstract).
proof_devices: SCIP solvers as independently running processes on subproblems (nodes of the branching tree) (abstract)
experiments: Up to 2048 cores of the HLRN II supercomputer; two previously unsolved MIPLIB 2003 instances solved (abstract).
positioning: SCIP described as one of the fastest non-commercial MIP solvers (abstract).

method_links.note: As in R014's card: platform reuse taken to its limit; the whole sequential solver is the parallel unit and inherits future progress. Same paper as R014.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: thin layer over the mature engine
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: SCIP solvers as independent processes; parallel development independent of SCIP; profits from future SCIP versions. Also on R014's card (same paper), so not a new occurrence.
Headline result: two previously unsolved MIPLIB 2003 instances solved. Existing candidate from D018 (c06); R014's card does not list it.

transferable: Build the parallel layer around complete solver processes and keep its code independent of the solver's, so later solver versions carry over with no change to the parallel code (abstract).
coauthors: Yuji Shinano, Timo Berthold, Stefan Heinz, Thorsten Koch

quotes.text: ParaSCIP uses SCIP solvers as independently running processes to solve subproblems (nodes of the branching tree) locally.
Thus, ParaSCIP directly profits from any algorithmic progress in future versions of SCIP.

title: Rounding and Propagation Heuristics for Mixed Integer Programming
contribution: An overview of eight computationally cheap rounding and propagation heuristics for MIP and a new performance measure, the primal integral, evaluated on MIPLIB 2010 benchmark instances (abstract).
problem_entry: Primal heuristics are an important component of MIP codes; the paper takes the computationally inexpensive ones, rounding and propagation (abstract).
key_idea: Assess heuristics by their ability to find feasible solutions, especially early in the search, with a new measure, the primal integral (abstract).
proof_devices: overview of eight rounding and propagation heuristics (abstract)
experiments: The primal integral and other measures on the MIPLIB 2010 benchmark instances (abstract).
limits_future: Not stated in the abstract. The published 2012 abstract keeps the claim to introduce the primal integral, so R017's attribution note (card c05) holds for this version.

method_links.note: For a primal component the payoff is redefined as finding feasible solutions early, with a measure of its own, not total time to optimality. Same paper as R017.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: measure designed for the component's job
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A new performance measure for the heuristics' job (feasible solutions early in the search). Existing candidate from R017; same paper.

transferable: When time to optimality misses a component's job (here: early feasible solutions), define a measure for that job and report it beside the standard measures (abstract).

quotes.text: In this paper, we focus on primal heuristics that only employ computationally inexpensive procedures such as rounding and logical deductions (propagation).
To assess the impact of these primal heuristics on the ability to find feasible solutions, in particular early during search, we introduce a new performance measure, the primal integral.

title: Stronger Inference through Implied Literals from Conflicts and Knapsack Covers
contribution: Extends SAT-style implied-literal detection to MIP conflict constraints and to knapsack covers, giving stronger inference from clique and implication tables, with gains in CPLEX 12.5 especially on harder instances (abstract).
problem_entry: Implied-literal detection improves SAT solvers on certain problem classes, in particular when applied dynamically to learned clauses (abstract).
key_idea: Carry implied literals over to MIP conflict constraints through the clique and implication tables MIP solvers already maintain, and extend them to knapsack covers with an efficient implementation (abstract).
assumptions: MIPs with conflict constraints and knapsack rows; clique and implication tables (abstract).
proof_devices: implied literals from conflict constraints through clique and implication tables (abstract)
extension to knapsack covers, with an efficient implementation (abstract)
experiments: MIP engine of IBM ILOG CPLEX 12.5; better performance, especially on harder instances; test set, measure and what makes an instance harder not stated (abstract).
positioning: Builds on SAT results on implied literals (abstract).

method_links.note: Clear at abstract level: a SAT technique moved to MIP through data structures MIP solvers already hold (clique and implication tables), then tested in the production solver.

transferable: Before porting a technique from another solver field, find the data structures your solver already maintains that can carry it (here clique and implication tables), then measure it in the full solver (abstract).

quotes.text: This results in stronger inference from clique tables and implication tables already commonly maintained by MIP solvers.

Our experiments show that implied literals, in particular through stronger inference from knapsack covers, improve the performance of the MIP engine of IBM ILOG CPLEX Optimization Studio 12.5, especially on harder instances.

title: Mixed Integer Programming: Analyzing 12 Years of Progress
contribution: Outlines an unbiased scheme for analysing benchmark results and applies it to the contribution of CPLEX 12.5's main components, a 12-year update of Bixby et al.'s analysis up to CPLEX 8.0 (abstract).
problem_entry: Bixby et al. analysed the performance impact of the main MIP features up to CPLEX 8.0 (2001, published 2004); Grötschel's 65th birthday is the occasion for an update (abstract).
key_idea: An unbiased way to analyze benchmark results, applied to the main CPLEX 12.5 components, with the deterministic parallel optimizer highlighted (abstract).
experiments: Test set, limits and measures not stated in the abstract. Per ZR 16-44 (co-signed): results grouped into solve-time brackets in a similar form (R021 p. 5); presolve-off degradation factor 11.4 in the >= 10 sec bracket at a 10,000 s limit (R021 p. 6); its Section 2 cited on test sets too small to conclude from (R021 p. 19).
positioning: Explicit continuation of Bixby et al. (2004) (abstract).
writing: Occasion-led opening: the two birthday celebrations (Padberg's 60th, Grötschel's 65th) frame the update (abstract).

method_links.note: The abstract names a scheme for analysing benchmark results and applies it to component contributions; Method 4 credits this paper with the bracket form, which the abstract itself does not show.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-measure a published number and explain the gap
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Re-measures Bixby et al.'s component analysis on CPLEX 12.5; whether the differences are explained is not in the abstract. Existing candidate (c06).

transferable: When a predecessor published a component-impact study, repeat it on the current code and state the analysis scheme before the numbers (abstract).

quotes.text: In this paper, we outline an unbiased way to analyze benchmark results and apply this scheme to assess the contribution of the main components in CPLEX 12.5 to the ability to solve MIPs.
We highlight some of the more recent features, in particular the deterministic parallel optimizer.

title: Presolve Reductions in Mixed Integer Programming
contribution: Describes the presolve of the Gurobi MIP code as a taxonomy of methods plus detailed descriptions of several techniques, some new to the literature, and reports presolve as a key factor in solving speed (abstract).
problem_entry: Presolve, which shrinks the model and strengthens the formulation, is a critical component in solving MIPs (abstract).
key_idea: A taxonomy of Gurobi's presolve methods, then more detailed descriptions of several techniques (abstract).
experiments: Computational results announced to show presolve as a key factor in speed, often the difference between intractable and solvable; no numbers in the abstract (abstract).
positioning: Novelty claimed for some techniques, with a to-our-knowledge hedge (abstract).
writing: Opens with MIP's breadth of applications before turning to presolve (abstract).
transferable: In a paper on a family of solver components, give the taxonomy first, then detail selected techniques and say which are new to the literature (abstract).
coauthors: Robert E. Bixby, Zonghao Gu, Edward Rothberg, Dieter Weninger

quotes.text: As our computational results will show, presolve is a key factor in the speed with which we can solve mixed integer programs and is often the difference between a model being intractable and solvable, in some cases easily solvable.

This includes an overview, or taxonomy of the different methods that are employed, as well as more-detailed descriptions of several of the techniques, with some of them appearing, to our knowledge, for the first time in the literature.
